name: git checkout
shortDescription: Switch branches or restore working tree files. A versatile but overloaded command — newer Git versions split its functionality into git switch and git restore.
detailedDescription:
The `git checkout` command has two distinct roles:

1. **Switch branches**: Move HEAD to a different branch, updating your working directory to match that branch's latest commit.
2. **Restore files**: Discard changes in your working directory by checking out a file from a specific commit or the index.

Because these are conceptually different operations crammed into one command, Git 2.23 introduced `git switch` (for branches) and `git restore` (for files). The `checkout` command still works and is widely used, especially for the `-b` shortcut.

When switching branches, Git updates three things: the HEAD pointer, the staging area (index), and the working directory. If you have uncommitted changes that would conflict with the target branch, Git refuses the switch and asks you to commit or stash first.

parameters.description: The branch name to switch to. HEAD moves to the tip of this branch.
Create a new branch and switch to it immediately. Equivalent to `git branch <name>` + `git checkout <name>`.
Like -b, but if the branch already exists, reset it to the current HEAD. Useful for recreating a branch from scratch.
Restore a file in the working directory from the index (staging area) or a specific commit. The `--` prevents file names from being interpreted as branch names.
Restore a file from a specific commit. For example, `git checkout HEAD~3 -- config.js` gets the file from 3 commits ago.
Create a new branch with no history (no parent commit). Useful for creating documentation branches (like gh-pages) separate from main code.

examples.title: Switch to an existing branch
examples.description: The most basic usage. Move to a different branch to work on it.
examples.code:
git checkout develop

# Git updates your files to match the develop branch

examples.title: Create and switch to a new branch
examples.description: The most popular Git command. Create a feature branch and start working on it.
examples.code:
git checkout -b feature-payment

# Equivalent to:
# git branch feature-payment
# git checkout feature-payment

examples.title: Discard changes to a specific file
examples.description: Revert a file back to its last committed state. WARNING: this permanently discards your changes.
examples.code:
# Discard changes in a file (restore from last commit):
git checkout -- src/broken-file.js

# Modern equivalent (Git 2.23+):
git restore src/broken-file.js

examples.title: Retrieve a file from a past commit
examples.description: Get a specific file from an earlier commit without switching branches.
examples.code:
# Get config.js as it was 5 commits ago:
git checkout HEAD~5 -- config.js

# Get a file from a specific commit hash:
git checkout a1b2c3d -- src/utils.js

examples.title: Checkout a remote branch
examples.description: Start working on a branch that only exists on the remote.
examples.code:
# Fetch remote branches first:
git fetch origin

# Create a local branch tracking the remote one:
git checkout -b feature-xyz origin/feature-xyz

# Shortcut (Git auto-creates tracking branch):
git checkout feature-xyz

commonMistakes.text: `git checkout -- <file>` permanently destroys uncommitted changes to that file. There is NO way to recover them. Unlike `git reset`, this modifies your working directory.
If you checkout a commit hash directly (not a branch name), you enter 'detached HEAD' state. Any commits you make won't belong to any branch and can be lost. Always create a branch first.
Modern Git recommends `git switch` for branches and `git restore` for files. These commands are less error-prone because they do only one thing each.
